When midnight struck Deke had found his remaining men lingering near the mass that was the 58th as a whole, it had become obvious that the art of flinging oneself out of a plane looked down on conventional military planning. Many of them had been wandering the island for a few days and participating in various training exercises, some of those exercises were still active, but with live ammo the men of Deke's own company would lead the next phase of the exercise. Observers from regular army training units were all around with their white helmets and orange vests to make sure the men wouldn't mix on accident, but the 58th had yet to have such a ridiculous mishap. When live ammunition was on the field they all took notice, and Fox Company did not pass by without glances from everyone else.

Marching took only a few hours, well ahead of schedule, which gave the men from the other companies time for some extra hours of sleep that they desperately needed. Deke was too wired to rest immediately, he always got this sinking feeling in the pit of his gut when out on exercise that reminded him of his childhood. When it was storm season his older brother would sit out on the cattle fence and watch them roll in from the Hibernic, they were far enough inland to be spared from the main wrath of the hurricanes but not from the winds and the rain.

Something about the memory of Toby sitting there, staring off at the horizon, made his skin crawl even as a grown man; he paced from the anxious feeling running up his back.

"Sawyer?"

For a moment he thought he saw Colonel Pierce standing in the doorway, but the man's broad frame and lit cigar was familiar for different reasons.

"Sir," he responded, snapping to attention with a salute. "Sorry if I woke you."

"Nah, sonny. Can't sleep either," General Ashcroft muttered. "Walk with me."

"Yes, sir."

They stepped out into the open gravel area that separated the range office and the large log wall that kept the firing lines isolated, the moon had come out and made their shadows long and sharp. Kerrick Island was quite beautiful, tropical, and the cool breeze from the sea made it absolutely pleasant. When he glanced at the general he could see that the man also agreed, it was hard not to take in the experience as they walked.

"Sawyer, let's speak frank. Where do you see yourself in five years?"

Ashcroft had the oddest questions sometimes, but he thought about it anyway. "I don't know, sir. With the way things-"

"Please, let's forget the politics for right now."

"Well... I do like it here in the 58th, I think the service is the right choice for me."

"Ever consider politics?"

"Me, sir?" Deke had to laugh at the suggestion. Then he saw the general's smiling face was quite serious. "Uh, no, it never came up in my mind."

Sawyers were already in the government, one of his more distant cousins had married into a political family. Deke didn't know the man quite well, his wife was the daughter of some old timer in the Yamasee Coalition Party that finally sent a senator to Harrisburg. Naturally he took up the mantle and entered into the fray himself, certainly not as a senator, but somewhere in that wretched town he knew his kin was laughing it up with the other fatcats.

"Neither did I!" the general laughed, shaking his head. "That's the real kicker, I wasn't even sure if we could figure out this damned tomfoolery of jumping out of planes."

"Sir?"

Ashcroft glanced at the younger man and smirked. "Did you really believe I came up with it? No, somebody threw me a bone... or maybe hung an albatross around my neck... hell, I don't know. Bumped up a pay grade and told, 'make it work,' but they left out the last part."

"The last part, sir?"

"'Or retire,' of course," he muttered, puffing on his cigar. "Jackasses didn't expect me to figure it out either."

That was well before Deke's time in the unit, but he had heard the legend of the unit's foundation led by their fearless leader who took on the fools in Harrisburg and told them what for. Few believed it happened exactly like that but he hadn't ever considered the political nature of the assignment, but thinking about it the signs were there. When they started out they were given the worst of the worst, the C-6 fleet they were using hadn't flown since the Islands War. Worse still were those damned commission rifles, his thumb ached just thinking about that finicky, uncooperative excuse for a rifle.

They didn't even have uniforms and had to scramble to find something they all could wear, finally they had to argue for permission to come up with something on their own. They had plenty of options available, but they decided to use old 1910 pattern trousers and blouse with provisions for their knee-high gaiters and parachutes. They stood out from the rest of the army, instead of a normal uniform caps they wore leather kepis with a peak in the front; somewhat like their grenadier cousins. Fellbaum had been poached from the 27th Grenadier Guard along with Weiss and Schumer; being from South Westrike all three of them spoke fluent German. Deke wasn't sure how Ashcroft had managed that, but the 27th was a regiment in their division so it probably wasn't too hard; Archer Company over in 1st Battalion was full of North Westrikers who weren't even in the army when they transferred!

Something about interstate agreements with the federal government... Deke couldn't remember the specifics of it. Regardless, they took to the job just fine and he imagined that was why Archer was their main rival in the brigade.

"Sawyer, I'm tellin' you this first on account of how you just got here but... They're probably gonna shut us down. I know your time's about up too."

"So that's why they've transferred one of my platoons away."

Shaking his head Ashcroft stopped walking and looked up at the mountain. "No, Sawyer. That was me. I'm probably going to cut the rest of your battalion too and keep the brigade as lean as I can to stay under budget."

Somehow that news didn't upset Deke as much as it should have, his whole life was the military and he enjoyed the perks it gave him. Respect was hard to come by in society, losing the 1912 war and the scandals that followed had put their reputation in the dirt, but he didn't much care about the opinions of civilians. They were like sheep, dumb, impressionable, and he was the sheep dog watching the shepherd mismanage them and spoil them while the wolves to the south circled. They were probably more envious of the wolves who dressed up like sheep and wined and dined with them than hateful of him, he really didn't feel much ill will toward the Espanian-speaking people under the boot of fascism.

Soon though, soon enough they would come to blows.

"Sir, if that's what you have to do then I won't hold it against you."

General Ashcroft smiled and nodded. "Sonny, I truly appreciate that. I do. I just don't want you to walk away thinking I'm some piker feeding you a line."

"My opinion of you, sir, is very high. If there's a way for me to help the unit just-"

"Oh I'm not... we're not finished, I've got a few cards to play," the general said with a puff of his cigar. "This election's put a damper on everything so I've got time to think."
